blocks.text:
Design a payment system, the system that takes a customer's request to pay a merchant and reliably moves money from one side to the other, through an external payment gateway such as a card network or a bank, while guaranteeing that a customer is never charged twice for the same request and that every single unit of money moved is durably, exactly accounted for. This is the first design in this category built around a hard requirement that no prior HLD problem in this project has had to satisfy: correctness here is not approximate or best-effort in any part of its core money-movement path, an error is not a bad user experience, it is a real, disputable financial loss.

The two techniques that make this reliable are idempotency keys, which make a retried request provably safe to repeat without double-charging, and a double-entry ledger, which makes every money movement self-verifying, since a debit without a matching credit is, by construction, always a bug.

blocks.text: A client should be able to submit a payment from a customer to a merchant and receive a definitive success or failure result. A retried request, using the same idempotency key, should never result in the customer being charged more than once. Every completed payment should be recorded as a balanced pair of ledger entries, a debit and a credit. The system should reflect the external gateway's own asynchronous confirmation of a charge, arriving later by webhook, updating the payment's state accordingly. A daily reconciliation process should compare the system's own ledger against the external gateway's settlement records and flag any discrepancy.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and every one of them is a hard requirement rather than a tunable trade-off.
blocks.content: Five qualities matter here, and every one of them is a hard requirement rather than a tunable trade-off.

blocks.alt: Exactly-once charging, strong ledger consistency, reliability under partial failure, PCI-compliant security, and full auditability

blocks.text: Exactly-once charging means a network retry, a client-side double click, or a timeout followed by a resend must never cause a customer to be billed more than once for the same intended payment. Strong ledger consistency means the fundamental accounting invariant, every debit has a matching credit, holds with zero exceptions, ever, since this is the number regulators and auditors ultimately trust. Reliability under partial failure means a crash in the middle of a multi-step payment must leave the system in a clearly recoverable state, never one where it is unclear whether money actually moved. PCI-compliant security means raw card numbers are never stored by this system at all. And full auditability means every money movement has to remain traceable, potentially years later, for disputes, chargebacks, and regulatory review.

blocks.text: This design assumes card data is tokenized by an external, already PCI-compliant vault, and this system only ever handles opaque tokens, never raw card numbers, covered further in section 21. The external payment gateway is assumed to confirm authorization synchronously but confirm final capture or settlement only asynchronously, through a webhook that can arrive anywhere from seconds to minutes later, which is why the ledger tracks both a pending and a settled state for money in flight. Idempotency keys are assumed to be generated once by the client and reused verbatim on any retry of the exact same logical payment attempt.

blocks.text: A payment platform at real scale can process tens of thousands of transactions per second at peak, each one producing at least two ledger entries, a debit and a matching credit, so the ledger itself sees several times that write volume. Gateway webhooks confirming capture or final settlement can lag the original request by anywhere from seconds to minutes, which the design accepts as a normal, expected delay rather than an error condition. A daily reconciliation pass has to compare millions of individual ledger entries against the external gateway's own settlement reports, a batch job sized for thoroughness rather than speed.

blocks.text: A payment request first passes through an idempotency store, which recognizes and short-circuits any retry of an already-processed request. A genuinely new request is handed to a payment orchestrator, which runs the payment as a sequence of saga steps, authorizing the charge through a gateway adapter and then posting a balanced debit and credit to the double-entry ledger. The external gateway's own asynchronous confirmation arrives later through a webhook receiver, which advances the payment's state further once capture or settlement is actually confirmed.

blocks.text: Every payment request carries a client-generated idempotency key. Before doing any real work, the system checks whether that exact key has already been processed; if so, it returns the original result immediately rather than charging anything new, making retries provably safe.

blocks.alt: An incoming request's idempotency key is checked against previously-processed keys; a repeat returns the original result untouched, while a genuinely new key is processed for the first time

blocks.text: Every payment transaction posts exactly one debit, money leaving the customer's account, and one matching credit, money entering the merchant's account, as a single atomic write. The fundamental invariant, total debits equal total credits, holds by construction, since the two entries are always written together or not at all.

blocks.text: A single payment moves through several steps across service and network boundaries, no single database transaction can span all of them, so the orchestrator runs it as a saga, a sequence of steps each with its own compensating action to undo it if a later step fails.

blocks.text: The idempotencyKey column on Payment is what the idempotency store's check ultimately relies on, giving the system a durable, queryable record of exactly which logical payment attempts have already been processed, independent of the in-memory idempotency cache's own retention window.

blocks.text: Money amounts are stored as integer minor units, cents rather than floating-point dollars, specifically to avoid the rounding errors floating-point arithmetic can silently introduce into financial totals. The ledger is append-only, an existing entry is never edited or deleted, a correction is instead always a new, offsetting entry, since a mutable financial record would defeat the entire purpose of an auditable ledger.

blocks.text: The happy path is the payment flow above, a new idempotency key, a successful gateway authorization, and a cleanly posted ledger entry. The workflow worth walking through separately is a saga failure partway through, if the gateway declines the charge, no ledger entries are posted at all and the payment is marked failed; if the gateway authorizes the charge but the ledger post itself then fails, the orchestrator's compensating action voids the authorization at the gateway, so the customer's funds are never held without a corresponding, successful internal record of why.

blocks.alt: A retried request with a still-cached idempotency key is served its original result instantly; one whose cache entry has expired is rejected, requiring a genuinely fresh key

blocks.text: The idempotency cache has a deliberately bounded retention window, long enough to cover any realistic client retry delay, but not indefinite, since keeping every idempotency key forever in a fast lookup path would be wasteful; the durable Payment record in the database, not the cache, remains the ultimate source of truth for whether a given logical payment was ever actually processed.

blocks.alt: Incoming gateway webhooks are placed on a processing queue and consumed by a worker pool that advances each payment's state in the orchestrator

blocks.text: Queueing webhooks, rather than processing them synchronously as they arrive, absorbs bursts in gateway confirmations without dropping any of them, and lets a slow or failing orchestrator update be retried safely rather than losing a confirmation outright.

blocks.alt: A transaction is routed to a ledger partition by hashing its account id, so every transaction touching one account is always handled by the same partition

blocks.text: Partitioning the ledger by account, rather than round-robin, is what lets each account's running balance be updated with strict, local consistency without needing cross-partition coordination for every single transaction.

blocks.text: The ledger is partitioned by account id and replicated for durability, since losing a financial record is never an acceptable failure mode. The idempotency store, by contrast, only needs to survive for its bounded retention window, and can be scaled more like an ordinary cache with a shorter durability requirement.

blocks.alt: The ledger's own debit and credit entries are strongly consistent, posted atomically or not at all; confirmation from the external gateway is eventually consistent, arriving asynchronously by webhook or later reconciliation

blocks.text: This split exists because the two pieces of state have fundamentally different owners, the ledger is this system's own record and can be made strongly consistent by design, while the external gateway's confirmation timing is entirely outside this system's control and must be treated as eventually consistent no matter what.

blocks.alt: A failure partway through the payment saga triggers the compensating action for every step that already completed, returning the system to a consistent state with no money lost or double counted

blocks.text: This compensating-action discipline is what makes a partial failure recoverable rather than catastrophic, at no point does the system have to guess whether a half-finished payment left money in an ambiguous state, since every step's own undo action is defined up front alongside the step itself.

from typing import Dict, List


# The outcome of a charge attempt: either genuinely new, or the cached result
# of an already-processed idempotency key.
class PaymentResult:
    def __init__(self, payment_id: str, status: str):
        self.payment_id = payment_id
        self.status = status


# One half of a balanced transaction: either a debit or a credit against one account.
class LedgerEntry:
    def __init__(self, payment_id: str, account_id: str, direction: str, amount_minor_units: int):
        self.payment_id = payment_id            # which payment produced this entry
        self.account_id = account_id            # which account this entry affects
        self.direction = direction                 # "DEBIT" or "CREDIT"
        self.amount_minor_units = amount_minor_units   # the amount, in integer minor units to avoid rounding errors


# A durable, append-only double-entry ledger: every transaction posts exactly
# one debit and one matching credit, so total debits always equal total credits.
class Ledger:
    def __init__(self):
        self._entries: List[LedgerEntry] = []   # every entry ever posted, never edited or removed
        self._transaction_count = 0

    # Posts one balanced transaction: a debit against fromAccount and an equal
    # credit against toAccount, as a single atomic operation.
    def post_transaction(self, payment_id: str, from_account: str, to_account: str, amount_minor_units: int) -> None:
        self._entries.append(LedgerEntry(payment_id, from_account, "DEBIT", amount_minor_units))
        self._entries.append(LedgerEntry(payment_id, to_account, "CREDIT", amount_minor_units))
        self._transaction_count += 1

    # Net balance change for one account: credits increase it, debits decrease it.
    def balance_of(self, account_id: str) -> int:
        balance = 0
        for entry in self._entries:
            if entry.account_id != account_id:
                continue
            balance += entry.amount_minor_units if entry.direction == "CREDIT" else -entry.amount_minor_units
        return balance

    # Verifies the fundamental accounting invariant across the whole ledger.
    def is_balanced(self) -> bool:
        total_debits = 0
        total_credits = 0
        for entry in self._entries:
            if entry.direction == "DEBIT":
                total_debits += entry.amount_minor_units
            else:
                total_credits += entry.amount_minor_units
        return total_debits == total_credits

    def transaction_count(self) -> int:
        return self._transaction_count


# Coordinates a payment: checks idempotency first, then posts a balanced debit
# and credit to the ledger only for a genuinely new request.
class PaymentService:
    def __init__(self, ledger: Ledger):
        self._ledger = ledger
        self._results_by_idempotency_key: Dict[str, PaymentResult] = {}   # idempotency key -> original result
        self._next_payment_id = 1

    # Charges from_account and pays to_account, unless idempotency_key has already
    # been processed, in which case the original result is returned untouched.
    def charge(self, idempotency_key: str, from_account: str, to_account: str, amount_minor_units: int) -> PaymentResult:
        existing = self._results_by_idempotency_key.get(idempotency_key)
        if existing is not None:
            return existing   # a retry; return the original result, post nothing new to the ledger

        payment_id = f"payment-{self._next_payment_id}"
        self._next_payment_id += 1
        self._ledger.post_transaction(payment_id, from_account, to_account, amount_minor_units)   # one atomic debit and credit
        result = PaymentResult(payment_id, "SUCCEEDED")
        self._results_by_idempotency_key[idempotency_key] = result   # remember this key's result for any future retry
        return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    ledger = Ledger()
    payment_service = PaymentService(ledger)

    # A genuinely new payment: customer pays a merchant 5000 minor units (e.g. $50.00).
    first = payment_service.charge("idem-key-1", "customer-1", "merchant-1", 5000)
    print(f"First charge: {first.status}, paymentId={first.payment_id}")

    # The exact same idempotency key is retried, simulating a client timeout-and-resend.
    retried = payment_service.charge("idem-key-1", "customer-1", "merchant-1", 5000)
    print(f"Retried charge: {retried.status}, paymentId={retried.payment_id}")
    print(f"Same payment returned, not double charged: {str(first.payment_id == retried.payment_id).lower()}")

    # A different, genuinely new payment for the same customer.
    second = payment_service.charge("idem-key-2", "customer-1", "merchant-1", 1500)
    print(f"Second charge: {second.status}, paymentId={second.payment_id}")

    print(f"Customer balance change: {ledger.balance_of('customer-1')}")
    print(f"Merchant balance change: {ledger.balance_of('merchant-1')}")
    print(f"Ledger totals balance, debits equal credits: {str(ledger.is_balanced()).lower()}")
    print(f"Total transactions actually posted (retry did not create a third): {ledger.transaction_count()}")

items: Architecture: an idempotency-checked payment orchestrated as a saga across an external gateway adapter and a double-entry ledger, with asynchronous gateway confirmation and daily reconciliation.
Capacity: tens of thousands of transactions per second at peak, at least two ledger entries posted per transaction, and a daily reconciliation pass across millions of entries.
The core techniques: idempotency keys for exactly-once charging, and a double-entry ledger with a self-verifying balance invariant, both worked through with a real, verified implementation.
Database: an append-only, account-partitioned ledger as the strongly consistent source of truth, alongside a bounded-retention idempotency store.
End-to-end workflows: a normal payment flow and a retried request flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: a strongly consistent internal ledger paired with eventually consistent, asynchronous confirmation from the external gateway.

Trade-offs: no idempotency protection versus a saga with compensating actions versus an unachievable true distributed transaction, compared directly on duplicate-charge risk and cross-service atomicity.
